hypothesis: The neuron responds strongly to **high-contrast, dark focal objects or voids** presented exclusively in **monochromatic grayscale**. The primary activating visual pattern consists of a **central, deep black or dark charcoal mass**—often a biological body (such as a spider, tick, or bird) or a geometric void (such as a window recess, eye pupil, or carved hole)—set against a **textured, medium-to-light gray background**. A secondary but prominent feature is the presence of **thin, radiating lines or appendages** extending from the central dark mass, seen in the legs of arachnids, the wings of birds, eyelashes, or radial splatters. The neuron is invariant to the specific semantic identity (biological vs. inanimate) and background texture (noise, stone, fabric), provided the stark **dark-on-light contrast** and grayscale palette are maintained. The activating feature typically occupies **10–50% of the image area** and is positioned centrally or slightly off-center.
